**Course Description**

*This course will critically assess empirical research on the causes and consequences of contentious politics, with a particular focus on efforts to address these questions using quantitative methods. The phrase “contentious politics” refers to group-based behaviors such as strikes, riots, street protests, or even terrorism and rebellion where participants make contested political claims outside of institutionally approved channels like voting or lobbying. What drives people to support or oppose these efforts? When are they successful and when do they fail? And how can we make scientific sense of something as seemingly chaotic as a mass protest, much less a violent insurrection?\
*

## Learning goals

By the end of the term, you should be able to:

1.  Define contentious politics and identify the major motivating questions and key theories in the field.

2.  Critically assess the methods and major data sources for studying contentious politics and have a sound understanding of their strengths and weaknesses.

3.  Collect, clean, and analyze data on contentious politics to produce original research on a real-world instance of contentious political behavior.

## Required Resources

-   [ELMS page](https://umd.instructure.com/courses/1390126)
-   A laptop with R and R-Studio installed.

Note that GVPT 201 is a prerequisite for this course, and I will be assuming some basic familiarity with using R, handling data, and interpreting statistical analyses. However, we will set aside class time to walk through examples of any code that will be required for this course.

## Components of the grade

### Participation and engagement (10%)

Attendance is a necessary, but not sufficient, condition for full credit here. Full participation means asking or answering questions, contributing to in-class discussions and exercises, offering constructive feedback on group projects etc.

### Homework Assignments/Quizzes (25%)

There will be homework assignments. These will primarily be used to reinforce in-class discussions on research methodology and will typically require a mixture of R programming and old-fashioned analytic skills to complete.

**As needed, I may assign unscheduled quizzes on required readings. These will completed in class and are designed to be free points if you’ve completed the required readings.**

### 2 Written response papers (30%)

Students will select two optional readings listed on ELMS and write a short response paper that summarizes and critically assesses the analysis and main findings of each paper.

### Final project/presentation (35%)

Each student will conduct a brief original analysis of a topic in contentious politics. This could be a profile of a single campaign or episode, multiple social movements in a single country, the use of a tactic in multiple contexts, etc. Your analysis should use a mix of both quantitative data (a pre-existing dataset and/or primary sources you have collected yourself) and qualitative data to support your claims. Your primary goal here is description (explain what happened) but you should also offer some explanation – however tentative – that explains why those things happened. Students will present preliminary findings in the last week of class and will submit a written (8-10 page) report on the final exam date.

**Late work:** [Unless you have a documented excuse](https://policies.umd.edu/student-affairs/university-of-maryland-policy-on-excused-absence) all assignments should be submitted online by the due date/time listed on ELMS. I will accept late work for partial (50%) credit provided it is turned in within 1 week of the due date.
